steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Every character has a motivation — what they WANT drives every action and line.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Super-objective: the character's overarching goal across the whole play; scene objectives are smaller goals within each scene.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Status: the power dynamic between characters — it shifts moment to moment and is shown through body language, position and voice.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Character arc: how a character changes from beginning to end — static characters stay the same, dynamic characters transform.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain the difference between a character's objective and their super-objective, using a character from a play you have studied. | How does an actor communicate a character's status change through performance? Give specific examples. | What is the effect of multi-roling on the audience? How must the actor prepare for this challenge?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Objective is the immediate want in a scene (e.g. to win an argument); super-objective is the overarching goal (e.g. to gain power). The character's scene objectives serve the super-objective. | Status is shown through: body language (high status = open, still; low status = closed, fidgety); spatial positioning (higher = more powerful); vocal qualities (pace, pitch, volume). Give a specific e | Multi-roling creates connections between characters, suggests social types, and challenges the audience. The actor must use clear physical and vocal switches — costume pieces, posture, accent, gesture

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always identify what a character WANTS — their motivation drives everything Track status shifts within scenes — they reveal power dynamics For multi-roling questions, discuss both the ACTOR's technique and the DIRECTOR's intention Character arcs matter — show how characters change across the whole play
